claim: Systemic blood coagulation accompanies inflammation during severe infections like sepsis and COVID.
source: Systemic blood coagulation accompanies inflammation during severe infections like sepsis and COVID.
evidence: This is a general statement about clinical observations in severe infections, supported by established medical knowledge and literature.

claim: During pyroptosis, the formation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) pores on the plasma membrane leads to the release of tissue factor (TF)-positive microvesicles (MVs) that are procoagulant.
source: During pyroptosis, the formation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) pores on the plasma membrane leads to the release of tissue factor (TF)-positive microvesicles (MVs) that are procoagulant.
evidence: This statement references the authors' previous work establishing the link between pyroptosis and procoagulant MV release.

claim: Mice lacking GSDMD release fewer procoagulant MVs.
source: Mice lacking GSDMD release fewer of these procoagulant MVs.
evidence: This refers to findings from previous research by the authors.

claim: NINJ1 promotes procoagulant MV release during pyroptosis.
source: Here, we show that NINJ1 promotes procoagulant MV release during pyroptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines.
source: Haploinsufficiency or glycine inhibition of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines, and partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Glycine inhibition of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines.
source: Haploinsufficiency or glycine inhibition of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines, and partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of NINJ1 partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
source: Haploinsufficiency or glycine inhibition of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines, and partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Glycine inhibition of NINJ1 partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
source: Haploinsufficiency or glycine inhibition of NINJ1 limited the release of procoagulant MVs and inflammatory cytokines, and partially protected against blood coagulation and lethality triggered by bacterial flagellin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inflammasomes are intracellular multiprotein complexes that detect pathogens by sensing pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: Inflammasomes are intracellular multiprotein complexes that detect pathogens by sensing pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Schroder and Tschopp, 2010 and Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014.

claim: The activation of inflammasome and subsequent pyroptosis are critical in host defense against pathogens.
source: The activation of inflammasome and subsequent pyroptosis are critical in host defense against pathogens (Miao et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; von Moltke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Miao et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; von Moltke et al., 2012.

claim: Pyroptosis exposes intracellular pathogens through plasma membrane rupture (PMR).
source: Pyroptosis exposes intracellular pathogens through plasma membrane rupture (PMR) (Nozaki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nozaki et al., 2022.

claim: Overactive inflammasomes are common in conditions like sepsis and COVID.
source: However, overactive inflammasomes, common in conditions like sepsis and COVID (Yap et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Vora et al., 2021; Sefik et al., 2022; Junqueira et al., 2022), can trigger systemic blood coagulation and tissue and organ dysfunction (Levi and Ten Cate, 1999; Levi et al., 2020; Al-Samkari et al., 2020; Giannis et al., 2020; Bowles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on sepsis and COVID.

claim: Overactive inflammasomes can trigger systemic blood coagulation and tissue and organ dysfunction.
source: However, overactive inflammasomes, common in conditions like sepsis and COVID (Yap et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Vora et al., 2021; Sefik et al., 2022; Junqueira et al., 2022), can trigger systemic blood coagulation and tissue and organ dysfunction (Levi and Ten Cate, 1999; Levi et al., 2020; Al-Samkari et al., 2020; Giannis et al., 2020; Bowles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on coagulation and organ dysfunction.

claim: Tissue factor (TF) is a membrane protein and the primary initiator of the coagulation cascade.
source: Tissue factor (TF) is a membrane protein and the primary initiator of the coagulation cascade, essential for hemostasis to stop bleeding upon injury (Morrissey et al., 1987; Mackman, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Morrissey et al., 1987 and Mackman, 2004.

claim: Elevated TF activity is associated with consumption coagulopathy in sepsis and COVID.
source: Elevated TF activity is associated with consumption coagulopathy in sepsis and COVID (Taylor et al., 1991; Levi et al., 1994; Pawlinski et al., 2010; Rosell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TF activity in sepsis and COVID.

claim: TF-positive MVs released by pyroptotic macrophages trigger systemic coagulation and lethality in experimental sepsis.
source: Our previous study has shown that TF-positive MVs released by pyroptotic macrophages trigger systemic coagulation and lethality in experimental sepsis (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous work, Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Pyroptotic cells undergo PMR at the late stage when the plasma membrane is beyond repair.
source: Pyroptotic cells undergo PMR at the late stage when the plasma membrane is beyond repair, where the blebbing and pinching of the plasma membrane releases MVs to remove membrane damaged by gasdermin-D (GSDMD) pores (Ding et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; de Vasconcelos et al., 2019; Babiychuk et al., 2011; Rühl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on pyroptosis and membrane rupture.

claim: The blebbing and pinching of the plasma membrane releases MVs to remove membrane damaged by gasdermin-D (GSDMD) pores.
source: Pyroptotic cells undergo PMR at the late stage when the plasma membrane is beyond repair, where the blebbing and pinching of the plasma membrane releases MVs to remove membrane damaged by gasdermin-D (GSDMD) pores (Ding et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; de Vasconcelos et al., 2019; Babiychuk et al., 2011; Rühl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on membrane blebbing and MV release.

claim: PMR could accelerate MV release as the entire plasma membrane is subject to being dissolved as MVs.
source: PMR could accelerate MV release as the entire plasma membrane is subject to being dissolved as MVs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the understanding of PMR and MV release.

claim: Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) oligomerization activates PMR during lytic cell death like necrosis and pyroptosis.
source: Kayagaki et al. recently reported that Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) oligomerization activates PMR, a process formerly thought to be passive, during lytic cell death like necrosis and pyroptosis (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021.

claim: PMR was formerly thought to be passive.
source: Kayagaki et al. recently reported that Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) oligomerization activates PMR, a process formerly thought to be passive, during lytic cell death like necrosis and pyroptosis (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is historical knowledge about the understanding of PMR before recent discoveries.

claim: Ninj1 haploinsufficiency inhibits the release of TF-positive MVs.
source: In this study, we show that Ninj1 haploinsufficiency inhibits the release of TF-positive MVs and provides protection against systemic coagulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ninj1 haploinsufficiency provides protection against systemic coagulation.
source: In this study, we show that Ninj1 haploinsufficiency inhibits the release of TF-positive MVs and provides protection against systemic coagulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reduced NINJ1 limits the release of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Reduced NINJ1 also limits the release of inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: A single dose of glycine injection has similar protective effects as Ninj1 haploinsufficiency by preventing PMR.
source: We find that a single dose of glycine injection has similar protective effects as they prevent PMR.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Total NINJ1 deficiency in the mouse strain used in this study caused frequent occurrence of hydrocephalus.
source: This approach was justified by our observation that total NINJ1 deficiency in the mouse strain used in this study caused the reported frequent occurrence of hydrocephalus (Kayagaki et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2023 and the authors' own observations.

claim: Flagellin is a PAMP known to activate the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome and trigger pyroptosis.
source: Flagellin is a PAMP known to activate the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome and trigger pyroptosis (Miao et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; Lightfield et al., 2008; Kofoed and Vance, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inflammasome-induced systemic coagulation is marked by prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and increased plasma thrombin-antithrombin (TAT).
source: Our earlier work has shown that inflammasome-induced systemic coagulation is marked by prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and increased plasma thrombin-antithrombin (TAT) (Wu et al., 2019), frequently observed in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation and COVID (Levi and Ten Cate, 1999; Levi et al., 2020; Al-Samkari et al., 2020; Giannis et al., 2020; Bowles et al., 2020; Iba et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and multiple other studies.

claim: Prolonged PT and increased plasma TAT are frequently observed in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation and COVID.
source: Our earlier work has shown that inflammasome-induced systemic coagulation is marked by prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and increased plasma thrombin-antithrombin (TAT) (Wu et al., 2019), frequently observed in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation and COVID (Levi and Ten Cate, 1999; Levi et al., 2020; Al-Samkari et al., 2020; Giannis et al., 2020; Bowles et al., 2020; Iba et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Intravenous injection of Fla activated systemic coagulation in Ninj1+/+ mice, demonstrated by a significant increase of PT and plasma TAT.
source: As expected, intravenous injection of Fla activated systemic coagulation in Ninj1+/+ mice, demonstrated by a significant increase of PT and plasma TAT (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice showed lower PT compared with their wild-type littermates when challenged with Fla.
source: Notably, when challenged with Fla, heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice showed lower PT and almost complete suppression of the elevation in plasma TAT compared with their wild-type littermates (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice showed almost complete suppression of the elevation in plasma TAT compared with their wild-type littermates when challenged with Fla.
source: Notably, when challenged with Fla, heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice showed lower PT and almost complete suppression of the elevation in plasma TAT compared with their wild-type littermates (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A single copy deletion of Ninj1 is adequate for significant inhibition of inflammasome-induced blood coagulation.
source: Our results suggest that a single copy deletion of Ninj1 is adequate for significant inhibition of inflammasome-induced blood coagulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing protection in Ninj1+/- mice.

claim: Ninj1 haploinsufficiency hindered the release of cytokines, as shown by decreased plasma concentrations of cytokines such as IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6.
source: We also found that Ninj1 haploinsufficiency hindered the release of cytokines, as shown by decreased plasma concentrations of cytokines such as IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The decrease in cytokine concentrations could be attributed to limited release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) due to less effective PMR in Ninj1+/- mice.
source: The decrease in cytokine concentrations could be attributed to limited release of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) due to less effective PMR in Ninj1+/- mice.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed decrease in cytokine concentrations.

claim: GSDMD facilitates IL-1β secretion into cell culture supernatant.
source: It's worth noting that GSDMD facilitates IL-1β secretion into cell culture supernatant and NINJ1 deficiency does not affect pyroptosis-induced IL-1β release in vitro (Kayagaki et al., 2021; Borges et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kayagaki et al., 2021 and Borges et al., 2022.

claim: NINJ1 deficiency does not affect pyroptosis-induced IL-1β release in vitro.
source: It's worth noting that GSDMD facilitates IL-1β secretion into cell culture supernatant and NINJ1 deficiency does not affect pyroptosis-induced IL-1β release in vitro (Kayagaki et al., 2021; Borges et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kayagaki et al., 2021 and Borges et al., 2022.

claim: Ninj1 haploinsufficiency did not change GSDMD expression.
source: Given that Ninj1 haploinsufficiency did not change GSDMD expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), there are likely unrecognized mechanisms in pyroptosis-induced IL-1β secretion in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are likely unrecognized mechanisms in pyroptosis-induced IL-1β secretion in vivo.
source: Given that Ninj1 haploinsufficiency did not change GSDMD expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), there are likely unrecognized mechanisms in pyroptosis-induced IL-1β secretion in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: Cell death, not the release of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β, is crucial for the over-activation of blood coagulation triggered by inflammasomes.
source: While our earlier research suggested that cell death, not the release of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β, is crucial for the over-activation of blood coagulation triggered by inflammasomes (Wu et al., 2019), these cytokines are vital for maintaining inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work, Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines are vital for maintaining inflammation.
source: While our earlier research suggested that cell death, not the release of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β, is crucial for the over-activation of blood coagulation triggered by inflammasomes (Wu et al., 2019), these cytokines are vital for maintaining inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of inflammatory cytokines.

claim: The release of inflammatory cytokines is affected by NINJ1.
source: Our findings indicate their release is affected by NINJ1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing decreased cytokine release in Ninj1+/- mice.

claim: Fibrin deposition in tissues can restrict blood supply, potentially resulting in tissue and organ damage and even death.
source: Fibrin deposition in tissues can restrict blood supply, potentially resulting in tissue and organ damage and even death (Levi and Ten Cate, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Levi and Ten Cate, 1999.

claim: Following the Fla challenge, fibrin deposition was noted in the lungs of wild-type mice by immunostaining with the fibrin-specific antibody 59D8.
source: Following the Fla challenge, we noted fibrin deposition in the lungs of wild-type mice by immunostaining with the fibrin-specific antibody 59D8 (Hui et al., 1983; Figure 1F), which was consistent with H&E staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No signs of fibrin deposition were observed in the lung sections of Ninj1+/- mice by immunostaining.
source: However, no signs of fibrin deposition were observed in the lung sections of Ninj1+/- mice, likely due to the technical limitations of detection on thin (5 μm) tissue sections, compounded by the potential of uneven fibrin distribution.
evidence: This is an observation from the study with a speculative explanation for the lack of detection.

claim: Fibrin deposition was detected in the liver and lungs of Ninj1+/- mice by immunoblot, but to a much less extent compared with their Ninj1+/+ littermates.
source: Using immunoblot to examine a homogenized whole lobe of the lung or liver, we detected fibrin deposition in the liver and lungs of Ninj1+/- mice, but to a much less extent compared with their Ninj1+/+ littermates (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ninj1 haploinsufficiency partially rescued flagellin-induced lethality.
source: Furthermore, Ninj1 haploinsufficiency partially rescued flagellin-induced lethality (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: NINJ1 protein plays a significant role in inflammasome-triggered fibrin deposition in tissues and lethality.
source: These findings underscore the significant role of NINJ1 protein in inflammasome-triggered fibrin deposition in tissues and lethality.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced fibrin deposition and lethality in Ninj1+/- mice.

claim: Systemic blood coagulation is a common complication of pathogen-triggered sepsis.
source: Systemic blood coagulation is a common complication of pathogen-triggered sepsis (Antoniak, 2018; Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Antoniak, 2018 and Tang et al., 2021.

claim: E. coli infection-induced blood coagulation was limited by Ninj1 haploinsufficiency.
source: Consistently with the findings from the flagellin challenge, E. coli infection-induced blood coagulation was limited by Ninj1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ninj1+/- mice exhibited a lower PT following E. coli infection.
source: As shown in Figure 2A and B, Ninj1+/- mice exhibited a lower PT and decreased plasma TAT following E. coli infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ninj1+/- mice exhibited decreased plasma TAT following E. coli infection.
source: As shown in Figure 2A and B, Ninj1+/- mice exhibited a lower PT and decreased plasma TAT following E. coli infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ninj1+/- mice had less cytokine release in response to E. coli infection.
source: Furthermore, Ninj1+/- mice had less cytokine release in response to E. coli infection (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Reduced expression of NINJ1 confers protection against E. coli infection-induced blood coagulation.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that reduced expression of NINJ1 confers protection against E. coli infection-induced blood coagulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing protection in Ninj1+/- mice infected with E. coli.

claim: The reduction in cytokine release in Ninj1+/- mice supports the role of NINJ1 in modulating the inflammatory response to E. coli infection.
source: In addition, the reduction in cytokine release in Ninj1+/- mice supports the role of NINJ1 in modulating the inflammatory response to E. coli infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced cytokine release in Ninj1+/- mice.

claim: NINJ1 plays a potential role in the pathogenesis of bacterial infection, including blood coagulation and the cytokine storm.
source: These findings highlight a potential role of NINJ1 in the pathogenesis of bacterial infection, including blood coagulation and the cytokine storm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing NINJ1's effects on coagulation and cytokine release during E. coli infection.

claim: Macrophage pyroptosis promotes the release of procoagulant MVs.
source: We have established that macrophage pyroptosis promotes the release of procoagulant MVs (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work, Wu et al., 2019.

claim: PMR during pyroptosis is the molecular event responsible for the release of procoagulant MVs.
source: We hypothesize that PMR during pyroptosis is the molecular event responsible for the release of these MVs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, which they test in the study.

claim: A significant reduction in PMR was observed in Ninj1+/- BMDMs, indicated by the decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the cell culture medium.
source: We observed a significant reduction in PMR, indicated by the decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the cell culture medium of Ninj1+/- cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), while cell death, measured by ATP levels, remained unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cell death, measured by ATP levels, remained unaffected in Ninj1+/- BMDMs.
source: We observed a significant reduction in PMR, indicated by the decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the cell culture medium of Ninj1+/- cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), while cell death, measured by ATP levels, remained unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NINJ1 mediates PMR but not cell death.
source: This is consistent with previous studies suggesting that NINJ1 mediates PMR but not cell death (Kayagaki et al., 2021; Borges et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kayagaki et al., 2021 and Borges et al., 2022.

claim: NINJ1 protein was detected in MVs released from Ninj1+/+ BMDMs.
source: Notably, we detected NINJ1 protein in MVs released from Ninj1+/+ BMDMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The protein level of NINJ1 was decreased in MVs derived from Ninj1+/- BMDMs.
source: The protein level was decreased in MVs derived from Ninj1+/- BMDMs (Figure 3A), likely due to reduced MV release and/or less NINJ1 protein in Ninj1+/- cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NINJ1 was detected in plasma MVs from Ninj1+/+ mice challenged with Fla.
source: Consistently, NINJ1 was detected in plasma MVs from Ninj1+/+ mice challenged with Fla (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ninj1+/- mice had decreased amount of NINJ1 from MVs, likely due to fewer plasma MVs.
source: Ninj1+/- mice also had decreased amount of NINJ1 from MVs, likely due to fewer plasma MVs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with a speculative explanation.

claim: The reduced quantity of MVs from both plasma and BMDMs in Ninj1+/- mice correlated with lower TF activity.
source: The reduced quantity of MVs from both plasma and BMDMs in Ninj1+/- mice correlated with lower TF activity (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: A decline in NINJ1 expression significantly reduces PMR and procoagulant MV release.
source: Our data illustrate that a decline in NINJ1 expression significantly reduces PMR and procoagulant MV release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced PMR and MV release in Ninj1+/- cells and mice.

claim: NINJ1-dependent PMR plays a critical role in procoagulant MV release.
source: These findings provide compelling evidence supporting a critical role of NINJ1-dependent PMR in procoagulant MV release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing the relationship between NINJ1, PMR, and MV release.

claim: MV shedding removes NINJ1 from the plasma membrane, hinting at a possible role of NINJ1 in cell repair.
source: Furthermore, MV shedding removes NINJ1 from the plasma membrane, hinting at a possible role of NINJ1 in cell repair.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that NINJ1 is present in MVs.

claim: It has long been recognized that glycine buffering protects against PMR during cell death, such as pyroptosis and necrosis.
source: It has long been recognized that glycine buffering protects against PMR during cell death, such as pyroptosis and necrosis (Weinberg et al., 1987; Estacion et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Weinberg et al., 1987 and Estacion et al., 2003.

claim: Glycine inhibits NINJ1 oligomerization and shields cells from rupture.
source: The exact mechanisms underlying the glycine protective effects remained unclear until Borges et al. revealed that glycine inhibits NINJ1 oligomerization and shields cells from rupture (Borges et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borges et al., 2022.

claim: Glycine injection led to a significant decrease in PT and plasma TAT.
source: Intriguingly, glycine injection led to a significant decrease in PT and plasma TAT (Figure 4A and B), demonstrating significant protection against flagellin-induced blood coagulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Glycine injection demonstrated significant protection against flagellin-induced blood coagulation.
source: Intriguingly, glycine injection led to a significant decrease in PT and plasma TAT (Figure 4A and B), demonstrating significant protection against flagellin-induced blood coagulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing decreased PT and TAT after glycine injection.

claim: Mice injected with glycine exhibited lower plasma MV TF activity post the Fla challenge.
source: Consistently, mice injected with glycine exhibited lower plasma MV TF activity post the Fla challenge (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Glycine buffering on isolated BMDMs protected against PMR, indicated by the reduction in LDH release.
source: In vitro, glycine buffering on isolated BMDMs protected against PMR, indicated by the reduction in LDH release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and decreased MV TF activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glycine buffering on isolated BMDMs resulted in decreased MV TF activity.
source: In vitro, glycine buffering on isolated BMDMs protected against PMR, indicated by the reduction in LDH release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and decreased MV TF activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Glycine-injected mice had higher MV counts irrespective of the Fla challenge.
source: However, we observed a discrepancy in MV counts between the in vitro and in vivo studies. Contrary to isolated BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), glycine-injected mice had higher MV counts irrespective of the Fla challenge (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Glycine might enhance MV release from cell types other than monocytes and macrophages, independently of inflammasome activation.
source: We speculate that glycine might enhance MV release from cell types other than monocytes and macrophages, independently of inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed discrepancy in MV counts between in vitro and in vivo studies.

claim: Glycine administration reduced the release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNFα.
source: Lastly, glycine administration reduced the release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNFα, consistent with previous research (Yang et al., 2001), but not IL-6 (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F and citation to Yang et al., 2001.

claim: Glycine administration did not reduce the release of IL-6.
source: Lastly, glycine administration reduced the release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNFα, consistent with previous research (Yang et al., 2001), but not IL-6 (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The cytoprotective effect of glycine buffering resulted in improved outcomes in inflammasome-induced blood coagulation and inflammation.
source: In conclusion, the cytoprotective effect of glycine buffering resulted in improved outcomes in inflammasome-induced blood coagulation and inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing protective effects of glycine.

claim: PMR serves as a pivotal molecular event responsible for the release of procoagulant MVs and the induction of systemic coagulation and inflammation.
source: In summary, our study employed both genetic and pharmacological approaches to inhibit NINJ1-dependent PMR. Our findings suggest that PMR serves as a pivotal molecular event responsible for the release of procoagulant MVs and the induction of systemic coagulation and inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data using both genetic and pharmacological approaches.

claim: NINJ1 inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy for reducing acute inflammation and coagulation-associated tissue and organ damage.
source: This novel mechanism sheds light on the potential for developing NINJ1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy for reducing acute inflammation and coagulation-associated tissue and organ damage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the therapeutic potential based on the study's findings.

claim: An anti-NINJ1 monoclonal antibody (but not the NINJ126-37 peptide) has been shown to prevent PMR, limiting tissue inflammation in mice.
source: In fact, an anti-NINJ1 monoclonal antibody (but not the NINJ126-37 peptide) has been shown to prevent PMR, limiting tissue inflammation in mice (Kayagaki et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2023.

claim: A single injection of bacterial flagellin does not replicate the evolving nature of a polymicrobial infection.
source: We do, however, recognize the limitations of our main model, as a single injection of bacterial flagellin does not replicate the evolving nature of a polymicrobial infection.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the experimental model used in the study.

claim: The flagellin model cannot offer insights into extended timelines beyond the brief period of flagellin-induced pyroptosis.
source: Consequently, it cannot offer insights into extended timelines beyond the brief period of flagellin-induced pyroptosis.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the experimental model used in the study.

claim: Heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice have decreased NINJ1 protein abundance.
source: We aimed to understand the role of NINJ1 on inflammasome-induced blood coagulation, using heterozygous Ninj1+/- mice with decreased NINJ1 protein abundance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Robust inflammasome activation and pyroptosis occurred in mouse primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) upon stimulating with purified Fla (LFn-Fla plus PA).
source: We confirmed robust inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in mouse primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) upon stimulating with purified Fla (LFn-Fla plus PA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Fibrin deposition in the lungs of wild-type mice after Fla challenge was consistent with H&E staining.
source: Following the Fla challenge, we noted fibrin deposition in the lungs of wild-type mice by immunostaining with the fibrin-specific antibody 59D8 (Hui et al., 1983; Figure 1F), which was consistent with H&E staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.
